newsitem.title: USA: Teamsters' Carey has high stakes in UPS strike.
newsitem.headline: Teamsters' Carey has high stakes in UPS strike.

text.p: Teamsters President Ron Carey Sunday abruptly ended high-stakes negotiations with United Parcel Service, even before a midnight deadline, and announced a nationwide strike affecting millions.
The strike threatens to cripple UPS, the nation's largest small package carrier and keep some 185,000 UPS workers off their jobs, but the personal stakes are high for Carey as well.
His rival for the presidency of the 1.4-million-member Teamsters union is still contesting Carey's election to a second five-year term in December.
The Carey campaign in June returned more than $100,000 in donations which James Hoffa, who had run against Carey for the top post at the nation's largest union, claims were illegal.

As a former UPS deliveryman and long-time president of the UPS local in the New York City borough of Queens, Carey also had a vested personal interest in the negotiations --- and little choice but to assume a tough posture in the UPS talks, experts say.

"He's got to produce," said Ben Burdetsky, professor emeritus and former dean of the business schoool at George Washington University. "This is a life-or-death issue for the membership and he obviously is going to have to back it."

Burdetsky said Carey's history with UPS put him in a slightly awkward position. "These are his people. He's got to back them, no matter what. He's got to win. You can't afford to lose that kind of battle," Burdetsky said.

Eager to keep the backing that got him elected as Teamsters president -- and vulnerable to the expectations of his local union -- Carey had less scope to manuever or back down in the talks with UPS than with other companies, he said.

Carey had sounded mildly optimistic at the start of Sunday's last-ditch talks to beat the midnight deadline and avert a potentially devastating strike, but when he emerged just over two hours later, he wasn't mincing words.
Negotiating further would be a "waste of time," he told reporters. "Somebody's got to stand up and say 'Enough is enough.'"
He said the issues involved -- a continuing shift from full-time to part-time work and UPS's use of outside subcontractors to do union members' work -- were immensely important.
"Part-time America just won't work. A half a job is not enough," he said.
Disappointed UPS leaders urged the union to let its members vote on the company's "last, best and final offer" themselves, rather than ordering them out for a strike.
Carey is no stranger to strikes and has a reputation for never backing down from a fight -- and union sources said he showed no signs of wavering in his determination now.
"This is important to him and he won't let go," said one union source.
